newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian death a reality check, says MP.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian death a reality check, says MP.

text.p: Australia's second voluntary euthanasia death would serve as a reality check for politicians soon to vote on a bill to overturn the law, anti-euthanasia parliamentarian Kevin Andrews said on Monday.
"What it does ... is that it makes it more real and people have to look beyond superficial claims about euthanasia and look at what the consequences are," Andrews told Reuters.
"That's the real import of the responsibility of members of parliament -- to look at what are the consequences in legalising lethal injections."

On January 2, Janet Mills, a 52-year-old cancer patient from South Australia, became the second person to use the voluntary euthanasia law when she ended her life through lethal injection, euthanasia campaigners said on Monday.
Andrews has moved a bill aimed at overturning the law, which came into effect in July last year in the lightly-populated outback region of the Northern Territory.
The anti-euthanasia bill passed the lower house of parliament, the House of Representatives, in December and will go before the upper house Senate early this year for final approval.
However, Andrews declined to comment on whether Mills' death was likely to impact on the final vote, which is expected to be close.
"People will come to their decisions for a variety of reasons and I can't guess that," he said.
Andrews said he believed Mills' death highlighted the fact that the Northern Territory law could be used by any Australians, not just residents of the territory.
"There can be no argument now that the Northern Territory law applies to all Australians," he said.
"The fact that she's a resident of South Australia quite clearly indicates that what the Northern Territory has done is made a law which applies throughout the Commonwealth."

He said he was also concerned that the law would be loosened over time to the extent that it would no longer be necessary for terminally-ill patients to get the required signatures from three doctors.

Leading euthanasia campaigner Peter Baume, professor of community medicine at the University of New South Wales, said earlier on Monday the Northern Territory should now amend its rules so that the medical specialist providing the third signature does not have to live in the Territory.

"On the day when we have the announcement of the second death, there's a demand to loosen the law further and a campaign to pressure doctors into participating in lethal injections and I think this shows quite clearly what will happen over a period of time if the law stands," Andrews said.
Mills' death followed that of fellow cancer patient Bob Dent, 66, who died through a computer-delivered lethal injection in September last year.
In Melbourne, Victoria State Premier Jeff Kennett told a news conference: "How else could you react but say she has exercised her right as a citizen.
"For people in those circumstances, that form of exit is, beautiful, and I trust that no federal government will ever meddle with the rights of people in such circumstances to make that choice,"
"I dont think any of us have the right to say that she shouldn't, If she wished, terminate her life."
